title: Kubernetes & kubectl
description: Exposing applications, health checks, graceful shutdown and packaging manifests.
resumo: Ingress routes HTTP by host and path through one controller; ingress-nginx is retired — prefer the Gateway API.
Readiness decides traffic; liveness restarts — never tie liveness to the database.
Graceful shutdown: Spring `server.shutdown: graceful` + `preStop` + a longer `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.
Helm: charts + values files per environment; `--set` only for what changes per deploy.
Kustomize: a base plus overlays in plain YAML; the `images` name must match the manifest exactly.

subsections.subtitle: Ingress: External HTTP Entry
subsections.description: Routing by host and path, with TLS.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a `LoadBalancer` Service creates one cloud load balancer per service, which gets expensive with many services.

**Concept:** an Ingress defines HTTP rules — by host and path, with TLS — and a single Ingress Controller serves all of them, routing to internal Services. An Ingress does nothing without a controller installed. ingress-nginx, the most used controller, was retired in March 2026 and no longer gets security fixes; for new clusters the Kubernetes project recommends the Gateway API.

**How it works:** `ingressClassName` says which controller handles the Ingress; the TLS certificate lives in a Secret.
examples.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [api.shop.com]
      secretName: api-shop-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.shop.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-orders
                port: { number: 80 }
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between a LoadBalancer Service and an Ingress?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An Ingress that no controller handles — none installed, or the wrong `ingressClassName`. It is accepted, but never gets an address, and nothing is routed.
examples.code:
kubectl get ingress
# NAME   CLASS   HOSTS          ADDRESS   PORTS
# shop   nginx   api.shop.com             80, 443     <- no ADDRESS

kubectl get ingressclass      # which controllers exist? use one of these names

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every rolling update produces a burst of 502 errors, and pods that start slowly are killed before they are ready.

**Concept:** readiness says whether the pod can receive traffic — while it fails, the pod is removed from the Service. Liveness says whether the process is stuck — when it fails, the kubelet restarts the container; never tie it to external dependencies, or a database outage restarts every pod. A startup probe protects slow-starting applications from the liveness probe. When a pod is removed, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and, in parallel, removes it from the Service's endpoints — for a moment it may still receive traffic.

**How it works:** enable Spring's graceful shutdown (finish in-flight requests), add a short `preStop` so the endpoints update first, and set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` longer than both together.
examples.code:
# application.yml
server.shutdown: graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s

# Deployment (container excerpt)
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40
  containers:
    - name: api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          sleep: { seconds: 10 }   # Kubernetes 1.30+; before: exec with "sleep 10"
      startupProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
        failureThreshold: 30
        periodSeconds: 5
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
examples.interview_question: How do you avoid 502 errors during a rolling update of a Spring Boot API?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A liveness probe that checks the database. When the database has a hiccup, every pod fails liveness and is restarted at the same time — turning a short database problem into a full outage. Dependencies belong in readiness, if anywhere.
examples.code:
# WRONG: liveness includes the database health
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health, port: 8080 }    # includes "db"

# RIGHT: liveness only checks the process itself
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the same manifests are copied for dev, staging and production with small differences, and installing third-party software means hundreds of lines of YAML.

**Concept:** Helm packages manifests into charts: templates plus a `values.yaml` file, with each environment providing its own values (replicas, image, resources). `helm upgrade --install` installs or updates idempotently, and each installation becomes a versioned release with history and rollback. It is also the standard way to install third-party software in a cluster, such as cert-manager or Prometheus.

**How it works:** `helm template` renders the YAML without applying it — useful to review what will change. `--atomic` rolls back automatically if the upgrade fails.
examples.code:
helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io
helm upgrade --install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace --set crds.enabled=true

# Your own chart
helm create api-orders
helm template api-orders ./api-orders -f values-prod.yaml    # render without applying
helm upgrade --install api-orders ./api-orders -n orders \
  -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=1.5.0 --atomic --timeout 5m

helm history api-orders -n orders
helm rollback api-orders 3 -n orders

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Overriding many values with `--set` on the command line. The real configuration of each environment lives only in someone's shell history and cannot be reviewed. Keep values in versioned files; use `--set` only for what changes per deploy, like the image tag.
examples.code:
# WRONG
helm upgrade --install api ./api --set replicas=5 --set resources.limits.memory=1Gi \
  --set env.DB_URL=jdbc:... --set ingress.host=api.shop.com

# RIGHT
helm upgrade --install api ./api -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=1.5.0

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** Helm templates are hard to read for a simple application, but copying manifests per environment duplicates everything.

**Concept:** Kustomize works with plain YAML: a base with the common manifests, and overlays per environment that apply patches (replicas, resources, image). There is no template language, so the files stay easy to read and review. It is built into kubectl (`apply -k`).

**How it works:** a good choice for your own applications in GitOps flows; Helm shines for distributing configurable packages to others.
examples.code:
k8s/
  base/
    deployment.yaml
    service.yaml
    kustomization.yaml        # resources: [deployment.yaml, service.yaml]
  overlays/
    production/
      kustomization.yaml

# overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
resources:
  - ../../base
namespace: orders
replicas:
  - name: api-orders
    count: 5
images:
  - name: ghcr.io/shop/api-orders
    newTag: "1.5.0"

kubectl kustomize k8s/overlays/production      # show the final YAML
kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/production
examples.interview_question: When would you use Kustomize instead of Helm?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An image name in `images:` that does not match the one in the base. Kustomize silently changes nothing, and production keeps running the old tag. The `name` must be exactly the image in the manifest.
examples.code:
# base/deployment.yaml uses:  ghcr.io/shop/api-orders:1.4.0
images:
  - name: api-orders             # WRONG: no match -> the tag stays 1.4.0
    newTag: "1.5.0"

images:
  - name: ghcr.io/shop/api-orders   # RIGHT
    newTag: "1.5.0"
